title: Preterite versus imperfect
objectives: I can choose between the preterite and the imperfect by asking whether the speaker presents an action as a completed whole or as a scene that is unfolding.
I can tell a story with a setting, a sudden event and a result.
I can describe what was happening when something else occurred, using 'estava' plus a gerund with 'quando', and two simultaneous actions with 'enquanto'.
I can explain why 'saber', 'conhecer', 'querer', 'poder' and 'ter' change meaning between the preterite and the imperfect.
I can give excuses and explanations with 'porque', 'por causa de' and 'felizmente'.
I can explain, from the rules of stress and spelling, why 'caí' has an accent and 'caiu' does not, and why 'escorreguei' and 'machuquei' are spelled with 'gu' and 'qu'.

vocabulary.note: 'Repente' is a noun for a sudden impulse, so 'de repente' is literally 'of-sudden', a fixed phrase. It introduces the event that breaks into a scene, and the verb that follows is in the preterite. Sounds: 'de' is [dʒi] ('d' before the sound 'i'), and 'repente' is [heˈpẽtʃi]: strong 'r' at the start of a word, nasal 'en', and 't' before the weak final 'e' becomes [tʃ].

example.target: De repente, a luz apagou.
example.source: Suddenly, the light went out.

vocabulary.note: 'Enquanto' is 'em' plus 'quanto' (in how much time) fused into one word. It joins two actions that run side by side, and both verbs go in the imperfect. Sounds: 'en' is a nasal vowel, and 'qu' before 'a' keeps a pronounced 'u', so it is [ẽˈkwɐ̃tu]. 'Lição' is written with a cedilla because 'ç' is the 's' sound before 'a', and 'ão' is the nasal diphthong.

example.target: Enquanto eu cozinhava, meu filho fazia a lição de casa.
example.source: While I was cooking, my son was doing his homework.
example.source_literal: In-how-much I cooked, my son did the lesson of house.

vocabulary.note: 'Naquele' is 'em' plus 'aquele' (in plus that) fused into one word, in the same way that 'em' plus 'o' becomes 'no'. 'Aquele' is the demonstrative for something far away in space or time. 'Naquele dia' sets a scene in the past, so it can be followed by either tense: the imperfect for how the day was, the preterite for what happened. Sounds: 'qu' before 'e' has a silent 'u', so na-QUE-le, with the weak final 'e' said [i].

example.target: Naquele dia, chovia muito e o trânsito estava parado.
example.source: That day, it was raining hard and traffic was at a standstill.

vocabulary.note: 'Hora' is hour or time, so 'na hora' is literally 'in the hour': at that very moment. The 'h' is silent. The negative 'não ... nada' is the normal double negative: literally 'not ... nothing'.

example.target: Na hora, eu não entendi nada.
example.source: At that moment, I did not understand anything.
example.source_literal: In-the hour, I not understood nothing.

vocabulary.note: Forms: 'caí', 'caiu', 'caímos', 'caíram' (preterite) and 'caía' (imperfect). The stem 'ca-' is followed by a stressed 'i', and a stressed 'i' alone in its syllable after another vowel is written 'í' so it is not read as a diphthong. In 'caiu' the 'i' joins the 'u' in one syllable, so no accent is written. The grammar note on spelling and sound works this out in full.

example.target: Eu caí da bicicleta, mas não me machuquei.
example.source: I fell off the bicycle, but I did not get hurt.
example.source_literal: I fell from-the bicycle, but not myself I-hurt.

vocabulary.note: The 'rr' between vowels is the strong 'r' sound [h], and the initial 'es-' is often said [is]. The 'eu' form of the preterite is 'escorreguei': the 'g' of the stem must keep its hard [g] sound before the ending '-ei', so a silent 'u' is added, as in 'cheguei' and 'paguei'. The 'chão molhado' of the example has 'lh' (said like the 'lli' of 'million'), and the 'ão' of 'chão' is a nasal diphthong.

example.target: Ela escorregou no chão molhado.
example.source: She slipped on the wet floor.

vocabulary.note: A regular '-ar' verb: 'quebrei', 'quebrou'. The 'qu' before 'e' is [k] with a silent 'u', and 'br' has a tap 'r'.

example.target: Caí e quebrei o braço.
example.source: I fell and broke my arm.

vocabulary.note: 'Ch' is [ʃ], like 'sh' in 'shoe'. The 'eu' form is 'machuquei' ('c' to 'qu', as in 'toquei'). 'Machucar' is reflexive when the person hurts themselves: 'me machuquei' is literally 'I hurt myself', meaning I got hurt. When the body part is named, the reflexive is usually dropped: 'machuquei o joelho', I hurt my knee.

example.target: Ele se machucou jogando futebol.
example.source: He hurt himself playing soccer.

vocabulary.note: 'Furar' is to pierce or make a hole, so 'o pneu furou' is literally 'the tire pierced': it got a hole and went flat. 'Pneu' begins with the cluster 'pn', a combination that Portuguese words do not otherwise start with and that is not said as in English 'pneumonia', where the 'p' is silent. Brazilians slip in a light vowel and say [piˈnew]. The 'ou' in 'furou' is a diphthong, said [ow] or simply a closed 'o'.

example.target: O pneu furou no meio da estrada.
example.source: The tire went flat in the middle of the road.
example.source_literal: The tire pierced in-the middle of-the road.

vocabulary.note: 'Faltar' means to be lacking, so 'faltou luz' is literally 'light was lacking': the light is the thing that is missing, and the verb stays in the third person singular. The 'l' that ends the syllable 'fal-' is said [w], so 'faltou' sounds like fow-TOW. 'Luz' ends in 'z', which is [s] or [ʃ] depending on the region.

example.target: Faltou luz no bairro inteiro.
example.source: The power went out in the whole neighborhood.

vocabulary.note: 'Levar um susto', literally 'to take a fright', is the fixed way to say to get a scare: 'levei um susto', I got scared. The related verb is 'assustar', to frighten, and 'assustar-se', with the reflexive, is to get frightened ('se assustou', got frightened). The 'ss' between vowels is always [s], and in 'susto' the 's' before 't' is [s] (or [ʃ] in Rio).

example.target: Levei um susto quando o telefone tocou.
example.source: I got a scare when the phone rang.
example.source_literal: I-took a fright when the phone rang.

vocabulary.note: 'Lh' is [ʎ], like the 'lli' of 'million': ba-RU-lho. The word ends in a weak 'o' said [u], and it is stressed on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in 'o'.

example.target: Ouvi um barulho forte na cozinha.
example.source: I heard a loud noise in the kitchen.

vocabulary.note: 'Uma notícia' is one piece of news, and the plural 'as notícias' is used for the news in general, where English uses an uncountable singular. Stress: no-TÍ-ci-a, on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so the accent is required. The ending 'ia' counts as two syllables, like 'história'. The 'c' before 'i' is [s].

example.target: Li a notícia no jornal hoje de manhã.
example.source: I read the news in the newspaper this morning.

vocabulary.note: Stress: TRÂN-si-to, on the third to last syllable, so the accent is always written. The circumflex is the mark Portuguese uses on a stressed 'a' before 'm' or 'n', and the vowel is nasal. After the prefix 'trans-' the 's' before a vowel is said [z]: [ˈtɾɐ̃zitu].

example.target: Cheguei atrasado por causa do trânsito.
example.source: I arrived late because of the traffic.
example.source_literal: I-arrived delayed by cause of-the traffic.

vocabulary.note: 'Atrás' means behind, and 'atrasar' is to put something behind: to delay it, or with the reflexive to fall behind ('me atrasei', I ran late). After 'chegar', the adjective 'atrasado' agrees with the speaker: 'cheguei atrasado' (a man) and 'cheguei atrasada' (a woman). The 's' between vowels is [z].

example.target: Atrasei porque perdi o ônibus.
example.source: I was late because I missed the bus.

vocabulary.note: 'Des-' is a prefix that undoes, like English 'un-' or 'dis-', and 'culpa' is guilt or blame, so a 'desculpa' is the lifting of blame. 'Pedir desculpa', literally 'to ask excuse', means to apologize, and 'Desculpa!' alone is the everyday sorry. Sounds: in relaxed speech the unstressed 'de-' is [dʒi]; the 's' ends the syllable, the 'c' before 'u' is [k], and the 'l' that ends the syllable 'cul-' is [w]: [dʒisˈkuwpɐ].

example.target: Pedi desculpa pelo atraso.
example.source: I apologized for the delay.

vocabulary.note: 'Por' (by) plus 'causa' (cause) plus 'de' (of). It is followed by a noun, never by a verb, and 'de' fuses with the article: 'por causa do trânsito', 'por causa da chuva'. The 'au' in 'causa' is a diphthong [aw], and the 's' between vowels is [z].

example.target: Por causa da chuva, a gente não saiu.
example.source: Because of the rain, we did not go out.
example.source_literal: By cause of-the rain, the people not left.

vocabulary.note: 'Sem' is the preposition 'without', and 'querer' stays in the infinitive because a preposition is followed by an infinitive, as in English 'without wanting'. Sounds: 'sem' is nasal, because an 'm' at the end of a syllable only nasalizes the vowel, and 'qu' before 'e' has a silent 'u'.

example.target: Derrubei o copo sem querer.
example.source: I knocked over the glass by accident.

vocabulary.note: 'Feliz' (happy) plus '-mente' makes an adverb, the way English adds '-ly': 'happy', 'happily'. The suffix attaches to the feminine form of the adjective, which for 'feliz' is the same as the masculine. 'Felizmente' is used in the sense of luck, so 'luckily' or 'fortunately'; to say 'happily' in the sense of with joy, use 'com alegria'. Sounds: 'mente' is [ˈmẽtʃi], with a nasal 'en' and 't' before the weak final 'e' becoming [tʃ]. No accent is needed, because an ending in 'e' is stressed on the second to last syllable by default.

example.target: Felizmente, ninguém se machucou.
example.source: Luckily, nobody got hurt.

vocabulary.note: 'In-' is a prefix meaning 'not', so 'infeliz' is unhappy, and 'infelizmente' is built like 'felizmente'. 'Pude' is the preterite of 'poder', explained in the grammar notes.

example.target: Infelizmente, eu não pude ir à festa.
example.source: Unfortunately, I could not go to the party.

vocabulary.note: 'Alívio' is relief and 'aliviar' is to relieve; 'aliviado' is an adjective made from the verb, so it agrees with the person: 'aliviado' for a man, 'aliviada' for a woman. No accent is written: a-li-vi-A-do ends in 'o', so the default stress is on the second to last syllable.

example.target: Minha mãe ficou aliviada quando eu cheguei.
example.source: My mother was relieved when I arrived.
example.source_literal: My mother stayed relieved when I arrived.

vocabulary.note: 'Des-' undoes and 'cobrir' is to cover, so 'descobrir' is to uncover: to take the cover off something hidden, which is to discover. It means finding out by discovery, whereas 'soube' means learning something from being told. A regular '-ir' verb: 'descobri', 'descobriu'. The 'c' before 'o' is [k].

example.target: Descobri a verdade ontem.
example.source: I found out the truth yesterday.

vocabulary.note: The basic meaning is to stay or remain. Before a feeling or a state it means to enter that state, to become: 'fiquei aliviado' is literally 'I stayed relieved', meaning I became relieved. The 'eu' form is 'fiquei': the 'c' changes to 'qu' so that it keeps the [k] sound before the ending '-ei'.

example.target: Eu fiquei em casa porque estava chovendo.
example.source: I stayed home because it was raining.

dialogues.title: Why were you late?
dialogues.context: Diego arrives late to work and explains to his manager, Sandra, what happened.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Diego, você chegou às dez. O que aconteceu?
lines.source: Diego, you arrived at ten. What happened?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.target: Desculpa, Sandra. Eu saí de casa às sete, mas o pneu furou no meio da avenida.
lines.source: Sorry, Sandra. I left home at seven, but the tire went flat in the middle of the avenue.
lines.source_literal: Excuse, Sandra. I left of house at-the seven, but the tire pierced in-the middle of-the avenue.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Que chato! E você chamou alguém?
lines.source: How annoying! And did you call someone?
lines.source_literal: What flat! And you called someone?

lines.speaker: Diego

lines.source_literal: I-called the insurance, but the service delayed. In-how-much I waited, it-began to rain.

lines.speaker: Sandra
lines.target: Nossa. E você não tinha o celular?

lines.source_literal: Our-Lady. And you not had the cellphone?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.target: Tinha, mas a bateria acabou. Por isso eu não avisei. Já pedi desculpa pro cliente também.
lines.source: I did, but the battery died. That is why I did not let you know. I already apologized to the client too.
lines.source_literal: Had, but the battery ended. For this I not warned. Already I-asked excuse to-the client also.

lines.speaker: Sandra

lines.source: That is fine. Luckily the meeting only started at ten thirty.

lines.speaker: Diego

lines.source_literal: What relief! Tomorrow I go to-leave more early, I-promise.

dialogues.title: You will not believe what happened
dialogues.context: Marina tells her friends Felipe and Carol about a scare on her bicycle.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Gente, vocês não vão acreditar no que aconteceu ontem.
lines.source: Guys, you will not believe what happened yesterday.
lines.source_literal: People, you not go to-believe in-the what happened yesterday.

lines.speaker: Felipe
lines.target: O que foi? Pode contar!
lines.source: What was it? Go ahead, tell us!
lines.source_literal: What was? Can tell!

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Eu estava andando de bicicleta no parque, ouvindo música, quando de repente um cachorro atravessou na minha frente.
lines.source: I was riding my bike in the park, listening to music, when suddenly a dog ran across in front of me.
lines.source_literal: I was walking of bicycle in-the park, hearing music, when of sudden a dog crossed in-the my front.

lines.speaker: Carol
lines.target: Meu Deus! E aí?
lines.source: Oh my God! And then?
lines.source_literal: My God! And there?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Eu freei, escorreguei e caí. Levei um susto enorme.
lines.source: I braked, slipped and fell. I got a huge scare.
lines.source_literal: I braked, I-slipped and I-fell. I-took a fright enormous.

lines.speaker: Felipe

lines.source: Did you get hurt?

lines.target: Felizmente não. Só machuquei o joelho.

lines.speaker: Carol

lines.speaker: Marina

dialogues.title: Did you know her?
dialogues.context: At a party, Helena and Bruno talk about Patrícia, the new boss, and what each of them knew.

lines.speaker: Helena

lines.target: Conheço. Eu conheci a Patrícia na faculdade. Eu sabia que ela trabalhava aqui, mas só soube hoje que ela é a nova chefe.

lines.source_literal: I-know. I met the Patrícia in-the college. I knew that she worked here, but only I-found-out today that she is the new boss.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.target: Eu também só soube hoje! Quando eu encontrei a Patrícia, eu queria falar com ela, mas ela estava ocupada.

lines.source_literal: I also only found-out today! When I encountered the Patrícia, I wanted to-speak with her, but she was busy.

lines.speaker: Bruno

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the new words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this unit can be read with rules you already have. The method from the lessons on sounds and on stress never changes: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, compare it with the default for the ending, and read each letter by its rule. This note applies that method to the words of this unit that are easiest to get wrong. The table at the end lists each one.

Start with the word that looks strangest, 'caí' (I fell). The verb 'cair' has the stem 'ca-' and, in the 'eu' form of the preterite, the ending '-i'. Two vowel letters make a diphthong, meaning one syllable, only when one of them is an unstressed 'i' or 'u' that glides against the other vowel. Here the 'i' is the stressed vowel, not a glide, so the 'a' and the 'i' are two separate syllables, ca-Í. That is called a hiatus: two vowels in a row that do not glide together. The lesson on accents gave the rule: a stressed 'i' or 'u' that is the second vowel of a hiatus, and that stands alone in its syllable or is followed only by 's', is written 'í' or 'ú'. This is what tells the reader not to read 'ai' as a diphthong, as in 'pai'. So the forms with a stressed 'i' alone take the acute: 'caí', 'caía' (ca-Í-a), 'caímos', 'caíram'. In 'caiu' the 'i' is followed by 'u' in the same syllable, which is the diphthong 'iu', so no accent is needed. The same rule gave 'saí' and 'saiu' in the lesson on the preterite, and it gives 'saía' in the imperfect.

Second, the spelling changes that protect a sound. The 'eu' form of the preterite ends in '-ei', and 'e' is a front vowel. A 'g' before 'e' or 'i' would change from the hard [g] to the soft [ʒ], and a 'c' before 'e' or 'i' from [k] to [s]. To keep the sound of the infinitive, Portuguese adds a silent 'u' or changes the letter: 'escorregar' becomes 'escorreguei' ('g' to 'gu'), 'machucar' becomes 'machuquei' ('c' to 'qu'), and 'ficar' becomes 'fiquei'. The same change gave 'toquei' and 'paguei' in an earlier lesson. Only the 'eu' form is affected, because the other endings begin with 'o' or 'a', which do not soften the letter: 'escorregou', 'machucou', 'ficou'. The same protection works in the other direction in 'conheço' (the 'eu' form of the present of 'conhecer'): the 'c' of the infinitive is [s] before 'e', and a plain 'c' before the ending '-o' would become [k], so the cedilla keeps the [s]. The verb 'frear', to brake, is a different case. Its stem ends in 'e', and the ending begins with 'e', so 'freei' has two 'e' letters side by side. Two strong vowels never form a diphthong, so the first 'e' is its own syllable, fre-EI, and 'ei' is the stressed diphthong. An ending in a diphthong such as 'ei' is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is written.

Third, the nasal vowels. In 'enquanto', 'sem', 'mente' and 'ninguém', the 'n' or 'm' after the vowel is not a consonant sound. It is the sign that the vowel is nasal, as the lesson on sounds explained. 'Alguém' and 'ninguém' end in '-em', which defaults to stress on the second to last syllable (like HO-mem), but these two words are stressed on the last syllable. They break the default, so they take the acute, exactly as 'também' does. The 'gu' before 'é' is one of the spellings with a silent 'u'. In 'felizmente', the ending '-mente' turns the adjective 'feliz' into an adverb, the way English '-ly' turns 'happy' into 'happily'. The 'e' at the end is weak and said [i], and the 't' before it becomes [tʃ], so the suffix sounds like MEN-chee.

Fourth, the words stressed on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts stress that far back, so these words always carry an accent: TRÂN-si-to (traffic), no-TÍ-ci-a (news) and Pa-TRÍ-ci-a. The ending 'ia' counts as two syllables, as in 'história'. In 'trânsito' the circumflex is the mark used on a stressed 'a' that is followed by 'm' or 'n', and the vowel is nasal. The lesson on accents treated 'ônibus' in the same way, and 'música', 'história', 'alívio' and 'ótima' follow the same reasoning.

Last, a few single words. 'Pneu' (tire) begins with the cluster 'pn', a combination that Portuguese words do not otherwise start with and that is not said as in English 'pneumonia', where the 'p' is silent. Brazilians slip in a light vowel: pi-NEU. 'Desculpa' begins with the prefix 'des-', so the 's' ends a syllable and the 'c' before 'u' is [k]: des-CUL-pa. In 'lição' and 'precaução', the cedilla writes [s] before 'a', and 'ão' is the nasal diphthong, which is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough. In 'furou', 'apagou' and 'faltou' the ending 'ou' is a diphthong, stressed on the last syllable by default. And two position rules apply again and again: 't' before an 'i' sound is said [tʃ] ('de repente', 'felizmente'), and the 'l' that ends a syllable is said [w] ('faltou' is fow-TOW). The remaining accented words in this unit follow rules from earlier lessons: 'aí' is a hiatus like 'caí'; 'sábado' and 'árvore' are stressed on the third to last syllable; 'braço', 'começou' and 'graças' use the cedilla for [s] before 'a' or 'o'; and 'chão', 'irmã' and 'então' are nasal words whose tilde also marks the stress.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the everyday words of the stories
grammar.explanation:
The previous note dealt with the words that are new in this unit. The dialogues and readings also use many ordinary words whose spelling follows the rules of the first lessons, and none of them is an exception. This note runs the same method on them: find the stressed syllable, read the default for the ending, and write an accent only where the two disagree.

First, short words. A stressed word of one syllable that ends in 'a', 'e' or 'o', with or without 's', takes an accent: the acute for an open vowel, the circumflex for a closed one ('mês', 'pôs'). That is why 'already' is 'já', 'only' is 'só' and 'we' is 'nós'. The accent also keeps a stressed word apart from an unstressed small word: 'nós' (we) against 'nos', a small unstressed word meaning 'us' that a later lesson teaches. 'Até' (until) and 'está' (is) end in 'e' and 'a', which would default to the second to last syllable, but both are stressed on the last, so they are marked: a-TÉ, es-TÁ. 'Vocês' ends in 'es' and would default to the second to last; it is stressed on the last, so it carries the circumflex, which also tells you that the 'e' is closed. 'Avó' (grandmother) ends in 'o' but is stressed on the last syllable, so it is marked, and the acute says the 'o' is open; 'avô', with the circumflex and a closed 'o', is grandfather.

Second, the tilde. It makes a vowel nasal, and when the word has no other accent it also marks the stress. In 'amanhã' and 'manhã' the final 'ã' is nasal and stressed on the last syllable, and 'nh' is a single sound, like the 'ny' of 'canyon'. In 'mãe' the 'ãe' is a nasal diphthong, one syllable. In 'reunião' and 'vão' the 'ão' is a nasal diphthong, which defaults to the last syllable, so the tilde alone is enough. 'Água' is written with an accent because the ending 'ua' is counted as two syllables, so the stress falls on the third to last, which no ending predicts; the 'gu' before 'a' keeps a pronounced 'u', as in 'quando'.

Third, the grave accent. In 'ir à festa', 'à luz de velas' and 'às dez', the mark records a fusion: the small word 'a' (to, at) meets the article 'a' or 'as' (the) and the two join into one long 'a'. It marks neither stress nor a change of vowel. The test from the lesson on accents works here too: you would say 'ao' with a masculine word ('ao hospital'), so a feminine word takes 'à' ('à festa').

Fourth, letter pairs that stand for one sound. 'Lh' is said like the 'lli' of 'million' ('filho', 'mulher', 'trabalhava'), 'nh' like the 'ny' of 'canyon' ('minha', 'manhã'), 'ch' like 'sh' ('chefe', 'chamei', 'chegou'), and 'rr' between vowels is the strong 'r' ('carro', 'bairro', 'correndo'). 'Ss' between vowels is [s] ('osso', 'passado'), so it is never a 'z' sound. Before 'e' or 'i', 'qu' and 'gu' have a silent 'u' and only choose the hard sound: 'quem', 'consegui', 'expliquei'. The 'h' at the start of a word is always silent: 'hoje', 'hora', 'hospital'. A 'j' is [ʒ], like the 's' of 'measure': 'hoje'.

Last, the spoken shortenings. 'Pra' is 'para' with its unstressed syllable reduced, and 'pro' is 'pra' plus 'o', so 'pro cliente' means 'para o cliente'. 'Tá' is 'está' with the first syllable dropped, which keeps the acute because it is stressed on the last syllable and ends in 'a'. They are written as they are said in informal speech and in messages; in formal writing you use 'para', 'para o' and 'está'.

grammar.title: Event or background: the two pasts
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has two simple past tenses where English has one. The English simple past ('I ate', 'I lived') covers everything, and English makes up the differences with extra words: 'was eating', 'used to eat', 'would eat'. Portuguese chooses between two verb endings instead. The choice is not about when something happened, because both tenses are in the past. It is about how the speaker looks at the action. A difference of that kind, which is separate from time, is called aspect. The preterite ('pretérito perfeito') takes the view from outside: the action is seen as one finished unit, with its beginning and its end in view. The imperfect ('pretérito imperfeito') takes the view from inside: you stand in the middle of the time and look around, and no beginning or end is in view.

A story has two layers. The first is the plot, the chain of events that move the story forward: I left, the tire burst, I called the insurance. Each preterite verb moves the story's clock to a new moment, so if the events are told in order, each one happened after the one before. The second layer is the background, which does not move the clock. It says what the scene was like: the weather, the time, how old someone was, how people felt, what was going on around the events, what people used to do. That is the imperfect. Two questions sort most sentences. Does this verb take the story to a new moment? Then it is the preterite. Does it describe the moment we are already in? Then it is the imperfect. A film is a good picture: the imperfect is the camera panning over the scene, and the preterite is each action in the plot.

Three facts surprise English speakers. First, length does not decide. 'Morei em Recife por dez anos' (I lived in Recife for ten years) is the preterite even though ten years is long, because the stretch is bounded: it has a start and an end, and the speaker sees it as one closed block. 'Quando eu era criança, eu morava em Recife' is the imperfect, because no end is in view. Second, counting decides. An action that happened a stated number of times is a series of complete events ('Fui lá três vezes', preterite), while a habit with no count is a background pattern ('Ia lá todo domingo', imperfect). Third, one verb can take either tense with a different message: 'A festa foi ótima' presents the party as a finished whole and sums it up, while 'A festa era ótima' describes the party as you remember being inside it.

Time words are hints, not rules. 'Ontem', 'de repente', 'uma vez', 'naquele dia' and 'primeiro', 'depois', 'por fim' usually go with events, because they fix a point or count a step. 'Antigamente', 'sempre', 'todo dia', 'enquanto' and 'quando eu era criança' usually go with the background, because they spread over a stretch of time. The verb has the last word. 'Ontem choveu o dia todo' presents the day as a closed block, and 'Ontem, quando eu saí, chovia' presents the rain as the scene for the next event. Both are correct.

Finally, a tendency. A state is a condition that simply holds (being tired, having a car, living somewhere, liking something); an action is something that happens (arriving, falling, opening). States are naturally background, so verbs such as 'ser', 'estar', 'ter', 'morar' and 'gostar' usually appear in the imperfect. Actions are naturally plot, so verbs such as 'chegar', 'cair' and 'abrir' usually appear in the preterite. This is a tendency and not a rule, since any verb can take either tense. The notes that follow show what changes when a state verb takes the preterite.

grammar.title: Combining the two: interruptions, simultaneous actions and sequences
grammar.explanation:
Two actions in the past can be related in time in three ways: one can happen inside the other, they can run side by side, or one can follow the other. Each relation has its own pair of tenses, and the logic comes from the previous note. A clause is a group of words with its own verb, and a conjunction is a word that joins two clauses (both terms come from the first lessons). The conjunctions in this note are 'quando' (when) and 'enquanto' (while).

An interruption is a long action with a short event inside it. Picture a long bar with one point on it. The bar is unbounded, so it goes in the imperfect, and the point is a complete event, so it goes in the preterite. In speech the bar is usually the imperfect progressive, which is 'estava' plus a gerund. The gerund is the verb form ending in '-ando', '-endo' or '-indo' ('dormindo', 'comendo', 'saindo'), and in Brazil the progressive is always 'estava dormindo', never the European 'estava a dormir'. So: 'Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou'. The clauses can be reversed without changing the tenses: 'O telefone tocou quando eu estava dormindo'. The plain imperfect works too ('Eu dormia quando o telefone tocou'), but in storytelling the progressive paints the scene more vividly. For the sudden event, 'de repente' is the usual signal, followed by the preterite: 'De repente, a luz apagou'. A start is also an event, which is why 'Começou a chover' is in the preterite: 'começar a' plus an infinitive means 'to begin to', and the 'a' is the preposition that links the two verbs.

Two actions side by side are two bars that run along each other. Neither has its boundaries in view, so both verbs go in the imperfect, and the connector is 'enquanto': 'Enquanto eu cozinhava, ele estudava'. The progressive is equally possible: 'Enquanto eu estava cozinhando, ele estava estudando'. If both were in the preterite, the sentence would describe two complete events, which usually means something else.

Two events in a row are two points. Both verbs go in the preterite, and the order of the clauses is the order of the events: 'Quando o telefone tocou, eu acordei' means the phone rang first and I woke up because of it. Compare how one change of tense changes the whole picture. 'Quando eu cheguei, ele saiu' means I arrived and then he left. 'Quando eu cheguei, ele estava saindo' means that he was already on his way out at the moment I arrived. 'Quando eu chegava, ele saía' (imperfect in both clauses) means that whenever I arrived, he was leaving, a habit. Portuguese grammar packs those three different stories into the tenses alone.

English maps onto this quite directly. 'Was raining when I left' is 'estava chovendo quando eu saí', and 'while I was cooking' is 'enquanto eu cozinhava'. The difference is that English uses 'was' plus '-ing' only for the progressive, while the Portuguese imperfect does the job of 'was -ing', 'used to' and 'would' at once, so the simple imperfect is often enough.

grammar.title: One verb, two meanings: saber, conhecer, querer, poder, ter
grammar.explanation:
Some verbs describe states that have no built-in beginning or end: knowing, wanting, being able, having to. The imperfect is the natural tense for a state, since it presents the condition itself as a background fact. The preterite presents something as a bounded event, and a state contains no event, so Portuguese reads the preterite of a state verb as the event at its edge: the moment the state began, or the moment it was put to the test. That single idea explains why one verb seems to change its meaning. English keeps the two meanings apart with different words ('knew' and 'found out', 'knew' and 'met', 'wanted' and 'tried'), so learners see a list of exceptions. In Portuguese it is one verb seen from two angles, and the meanings can be worked out instead of memorized.

'Saber' means to know a fact or to know how to do something. 'Sabia' is the state of knowing, and 'soube' is the moment the knowing began: 'found out'. 'Conhecer' means to be acquainted with a person, a place or a thing, as opposed to knowing a fact. 'Conhecia' is the state of being acquainted, and 'conheci' is the moment the acquaintance began: 'met for the first time'. 'Querer' means to want. 'Queria' is the state of wanting, with no claim that anything was done about it. 'Quis' means that the wish was acted on: I tried, or I decided. In the negative, 'não quis' means that the wish was tested and the answer was no: I refused. 'Poder' means to be able. 'Podia' is the state of being able and says nothing about whether it happened: 'Eu podia ir, mas não fui', I could have gone, but I did not. 'Pude' means that the ability was used: I managed to. 'Não pude' means that on that occasion I tried and was unable. 'Ter que', the usual way to say 'have to', follows the same logic: 'tinha que' is the state of being obliged, and leaves open whether you did it; 'tive que' says that the obligation was carried out: 'had to, and did'. Finally, 'ter': 'tinha' is simply 'had' (a car, a cold), while 'tive' is 'got' or 'had' as an experience: 'Tive notícias boas' means 'I got good news'.

The forms are not new. 'Soube', 'pude', 'quis' and 'tive' are the irregular preterite stems from the earlier lesson, and 'sabia', 'conhecia', 'queria' and 'podia' are regular imperfects ('tinha' is one of the four irregular imperfects). What is new is the meaning. In the imperfect, 'queria' also serves as a polite request ('Eu queria um café'): the wish is kept in the background and not pressed on the listener. And 'soube' is not the only way to say 'found out': 'descobri' is used when you found out by discovering something, and 'soube' when you learned it by being told.

grammar.title: Building a story and giving explanations
grammar.explanation:
A story has a shape, and each part has its tense. First comes the setting, in the imperfect: 'Era sábado, chovia e eu estava em casa'. Then the trigger, in the preterite, often introduced by 'de repente' or 'quando': 'De repente, faltou luz'. Then the reaction and the result, in the preterite: 'Levei um susto, mas felizmente ninguém se machucou'. Feelings follow the same logic as the verbs in the previous note, and here 'estar' and 'ficar' show it. 'Eu estava nervoso' describes the state (imperfect). 'Fiquei nervoso' says that the state began (preterite), because 'ficar' means to become. 'Ficar' is literally 'to stay', and before a feeling it means to stay in the state that you have just entered, so 'fiquei aliviado' is literally 'I stayed relieved', that is, I became relieved.

To give a reason, Portuguese has three tools, and the difference is what follows. 'Porque' (one word, no accent) introduces a clause: 'Atrasei porque perdi o ônibus'. 'Por causa de' introduces a noun: 'Por causa do trânsito, cheguei atrasado'. 'Por isso', literally 'for this', gives the result: 'Perdi o ônibus, por isso me atrasei'. The tense inside the reason follows the usual logic. A reason that is an event is in the preterite ('porque perdi o ônibus'), and a reason that is a continuing state is in the imperfect ('Não atendi porque estava dormindo').

The question word is written differently. 'Por que' (two words, no accent) begins a question: 'Por que você se atrasou?' At the end of a question, the last word takes an accent: 'Você se atrasou por quê?' One word with an accent, 'porquê', is a noun meaning 'the reason': 'Não entendi o porquê'. And 'porque', one word without an accent, is the answer to the question, meaning 'because'. English uses 'why' and 'because', which never look alike, so the spelling is the only thing to learn here.

In Brazilian speech an explanation often starts with 'Desculpa!' (sorry), and when you report the apology later you use 'Pedi desculpa', I apologized. 'Nossa' and 'Meu Deus' are the usual reactions to surprising news, and 'Ainda bem' means 'thank goodness'.

culture.title: Trânsito, desculpas and good stories
culture.text:
In big Brazilian cities, the most common excuse for being late is 'o trânsito'. In São Paulo or Rio de Janeiro, people really do spend hours commuting, so colleagues usually accept it. Saying 'Desculpa o atraso, o trânsito estava um caos' is normal and polite. Literally it is 'excuse the delay, the traffic was a chaos', and 'estava' is in the imperfect because the traffic is the scene, not an event. Punctuality is generally more flexible than in some other countries, especially for social events, but for work meetings and appointments it is still important to warn people, often with a quick WhatsApp message like 'Estou chegando, cinco minutinhos'. The ending '-inho', which appears here as '-inhos' ('nh' is the sound of 'ny' in 'canyon'), makes a word small or affectionate, so 'cinco minutinhos' is a friendly 'five little minutes'.

Brazilians love to tell stories, and the way they tell them is lively. People use many reactions. 'Nossa!' is short for 'Nossa Senhora', literally 'Our Lady', and works like 'wow'. 'Meu Deus!' is 'my God', 'Que susto!' is 'what a scare', 'Ufa!' is 'phew', and 'Graças a Deus' is 'thanks to God'. 'Ainda bem!' is literally 'still well', and it means 'thank goodness': something could have gone badly, and it did not. Short voice messages on WhatsApp, called 'áudios', are often used to tell a full story in a minute or two, and the listener answers with laughing or surprised reactions. A good story includes details of the scene and a sudden turn, which is exactly the structure of imperfect and preterite.

News reports follow a similar style. On television and in newspapers, a short report normally starts with the facts in the preterite, 'Um ciclista caiu na tarde de ontem', and then gives the context in the imperfect, 'Ele andava pela ciclovia quando um cachorro atravessou'. Learning to read these texts is an excellent way to practice the contrast between the two tenses.

She hurt her knee a little but did not break any bone.

questions.prompt: Why did the dog run off, according to the owner?
choices: It was frightened by a noise.
questions.explanation: O animal se assustou com um barulho.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, why is 'andava' in the imperfect and 'atravessou' in the preterite?
choices: 'Andava' is the long action in progress, and 'atravessou' is the sudden event that interrupted it
'Andava' is a habit, and 'atravessou' is a feeling
Both are events that happened one after the other
'Atravessou' is the background and 'andava' is the plot
questions.explanation: The imperfect is the stretch of time already under way, and the preterite is the point that breaks into it.

exercises.prompt: Match the verb form with its meaning in a story

pairs.source: I met for the first time

exercises.explanation: In each pair the preterite names the moment a state began or was acted on, and the imperfect names the state itself.

exercises.prompt: What does the choice between the preterite and the imperfect depend on?
choices: How long ago the action happened
Whether the speaker presents the action as a completed whole or as a scene in progress
Whether the verb ends in '-ar', '-er' or '-ir'
exercises.explanation: Both tenses are past. The difference is aspect: the preterite views the action from outside as a unit, and the imperfect views it from inside as something unfolding.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence moves the story forward to a new moment?
exercises.explanation: 'Faltou' is a preterite event. The other three are imperfect and describe the scene.

exercises.prompt: De repente, a luz ___.
exercises.explanation: A sudden event that moves the story forward is in the preterite.

exercises.prompt_target: Eu ___ dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
exercises.hint_source: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
exercises.explanation: The long action in progress is the imperfect progressive, 'estava' plus a gerund. The short interruption, 'tocou', is the preterite.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I was sleeping when the phone rang'?
choices: Eu dormi quando o telefone tocava.
Eu dormia quando o telefone toca.
Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocando.
exercises.explanation: The ongoing background is imperfect, and the sudden interruption is preterite. A gerund such as 'tocando' cannot replace a conjugated verb here.

exercises.prompt_target: De repente, o cachorro ___ na minha frente.
exercises.hint_source: Suddenly, the dog crossed in front of me.
exercises.explanation: 'De repente' introduces an event, so the verb is in the preterite.

exercises.audio_target: De repente, ouvi um barulho forte.
choices: Suddenly, I saw a bright light.
Suddenly, I felt a strong wind.
Suddenly, I heard a loud noise.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'morei' (preterite) correct in 'Morei em Recife por dez anos'?
choices: Because ten years is a short time
Because the sentence is about the present
Because ten years is a bounded stretch with a start and an end, seen as one closed block
exercises.explanation: Length does not decide the tense. A stretch that is bounded and seen as a whole takes the preterite, however long it is.

exercises.prompt_target: Ano passado eu ___ ao Rio três vezes.
exercises.hint_source: Last year I went to Rio three times.
exercises.explanation: An action counted a specific number of times is a series of complete events, so the preterite is used. 'Fui' is the preterite of 'ir'.

exercises.prompt_target: Todo domingo a gente ___ à casa da minha avó.
exercises.hint_source: Every Sunday we used to go to my grandmother's house.
exercises.explanation: A repeated habit with no count and no end in view is background, so the imperfect is used. 'Ia' is the imperfect of 'ir'.

exercises.audio_target: Levei um susto quando o telefone tocou.
exercises.hint_source: I got a scare when the phone rang.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Ontem eu soube que ele viajou' mean?
choices: I found out that he traveled.
exercises.explanation: 'Soube' is the preterite of 'saber'. The state of knowing is seen at its edge, the moment it began, so it means 'found out'.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'caí' written with an accent but 'caiu' is not?
choices: Every word that ends in 'i' needs an accent
'Caí' is the plural and 'caiu' is the singular
'Caí' is stressed on the first syllable and 'caiu' on the last
In 'caí' the stressed 'i' is alone in its syllable after the 'a', a hiatus, so it takes the acute; in 'caiu' the 'i' and 'u' form one diphthong
exercises.explanation: A stressed 'i' or 'u' that is the second vowel of a hiatus and stands alone in its syllable is written 'í' or 'ú'. In 'caiu' the 'i' is followed by 'u' in the same syllable, so there is no accent.

exercises.prompt_target: Eu ___ da bicicleta, mas não me machuquei.
exercises.hint_source: I fell off the bicycle, but I did not get hurt.
exercises.explanation: The 'eu' form of the preterite of 'cair' is 'caí', with the acute on the stressed 'i' that stands alone after the 'a'.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'escorreguei' spelled with 'gu'?
choices: The 'g' must keep its hard sound before the ending '-ei', so a silent 'u' is added
exercises.explanation: A 'g' before 'e' or 'i' would become the soft [ʒ]. The silent 'u' keeps the [g] of the infinitive, as in 'cheguei' and 'paguei'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'trânsito' carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so the accent is always written
It is stressed on the last syllable
It ends in 'o', and every word ending in 'o' needs an accent
The tilde was replaced by the circumflex in 2009
exercises.explanation: TRÂN-si-to is a word stressed on the third to last syllable, and such words always carry an accent.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'nós' (we) written with an accent, while 'nos' (us) is not?
choices: A stressed word of one syllable ending in 'o' plus 's' takes the acute, which keeps it apart from the unstressed small word 'nos'
'Nós' is a verb form and 'nos' is a noun
The accent shows a nasal vowel
exercises.explanation: Stressed one-syllable words ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' (with or without 's') are marked, as in 'já', 'só' and 'nós'. 'Nos' is unstressed, so it is left bare.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'ninguém' carry an accent when 'homem' does not?
choices: 'Ninguém' is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for an ending in 'em'; 'homem' is stressed on the second to last, as the default predicts
'Homem' has a silent 'h', which cancels the accent
The accent on 'ninguém' shows that the 'g' is hard
exercises.explanation: An ending in 'em' defaults to the second to last syllable (HO-mem). A word with the same ending stressed on the last syllable (nin-GUÉM, 'também') must be marked.

exercises.prompt: What does the accent in 'ir à festa' record?
choices: That the small word 'a' (to) has fused with the article 'a' (the)
exercises.explanation: The grave accent has one job, 'crase': a fusion of the preposition 'a' and the article 'a' or 'as'. It marks neither stress nor a change of sound.

exercises.prompt: In 'Pedi desculpa pro cliente', what is 'pro'?
choices: A spoken shortening of 'para o', meaning 'to the'
A spoken shortening of 'por o', meaning 'by the'
exercises.explanation: 'Pra' is 'para' reduced, and 'pro' is 'pra' plus 'o'. Both are normal in informal speech and messages; formal writing uses 'para' and 'para o'.

exercises.audio_target: O pneu furou no meio da estrada.
choices: The engine stopped in the middle of the road.
The door opened in the middle of the road.
The tire went flat in the middle of the road.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Quando eu cheguei, ele saiu' and 'Quando eu cheguei, ele estava saindo'?
choices: In the first he left after I arrived; in the second he was already leaving when I arrived
The first is about the future
In the second I was the one leaving
exercises.explanation: Two preterites are two events in sequence. The imperfect progressive is the long action that the preterite arrived inside.

exercises.prompt_target: Enquanto eu ___ o jantar, meu filho fazia a lição.
exercises.hint_source: While I was preparing dinner, my son was doing his homework.
exercises.explanation: Two actions running side by side, joined by 'enquanto', are both imperfect.

exercises.prompt_source: We were chatting when the light went out.

exercises.prompt_target: Tentei abrir a porta, mas não ___.
exercises.hint_source: I tried to open the door, but I could not.
exercises.explanation: 'Não pude' says that on that occasion the ability was put to the test and failed.

exercises.prompt_target: Eu já ___ a resposta, mas não queria falar.
exercises.hint_source: I already knew the answer, but I did not want to say it.
exercises.explanation: Knowing something is a state, and a state in the background is the imperfect.

exercises.prompt: 'Eu não quis ir à festa'. What does this mean?
choices: I refused to go to the party.
I could not go to the party.
I did not know about the party.
I was going to the party.
exercises.explanation: The preterite of 'querer' is the wish acted on. In the negative it means that you refused.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says you met Ana for the first time?
exercises.explanation: 'Conheci' is the preterite: the moment the acquaintance began.

exercises.audio_target: Eu sabia a resposta, mas não quis falar.
exercises.hint_source: I knew the answer, but I refused to say it.

exercises.prompt: Qual palavra liga duas ações que acontecem ao mesmo tempo?
exercises.explanation: 'Enquanto', literally 'in-how-much', joins two actions that run side by side.

exercises.prompt_target: Quando eu saí de casa, ___ muito frio.
exercises.hint_source: When I left home, it was very cold.
exercises.explanation: Weather as background is in the imperfect: 'fazia frio' or 'estava frio'.

exercises.prompt_target: Quando a luz voltou, eu ___ aliviado.
exercises.hint_source: When the power came back, I became relieved.
exercises.explanation: 'Ficar' means to become, so the preterite 'fiquei' marks the moment the feeling began. 'Estava' would describe the feeling as a state already there.

exercises.prompt_target: O copo caiu e ___ no chão.
exercises.hint_source: The glass fell and broke on the floor.
exercises.explanation: A second event in the chain, so the preterite. 'Quebrar' is a regular '-ar' verb: 'quebrou'.

exercises.prompt_source: I was walking when it started to rain.
answers: Eu estava andando quando começou a chover.
Estava andando quando começou a chover.
Eu estava caminhando quando começou a chover.
Eu caminhava quando começou a chover.
Quando começou a chover, eu estava caminhando.
Estava caminhando quando começou a chover.
Eu andava quando começou a chover.
Eu estava andando quando a chuva começou.
Quando começou a chover, eu estava andando.
exercises.explanation: The walking is the long action in progress and the start of the rain is the event.

exercises.prompt_source: When I arrived, she was leaving.
answers: Quando eu cheguei, ela estava saindo.
Ela estava saindo quando eu cheguei.
exercises.explanation: Her leaving is already in progress, so 'estava saindo'; my arrival is the event, so 'cheguei'.

exercises.prompt: Which option completes the sentence: '___ trânsito, cheguei atrasado'.
exercises.explanation: 'Por causa de' introduces a noun and fuses with the article: 'por causa do trânsito'. 'Porque' introduces a clause with its own verb.

exercises.prompt_source: I arrived late because I missed the bus.
answers: Cheguei atrasado porque perdi o ônibus.
Cheguei atrasada porque perdi o ônibus.
Eu cheguei atrasado porque perdi o ônibus.
Eu cheguei atrasada porque perdi o ônibus.
Cheguei atrasado porque eu perdi o ônibus.
Cheguei atrasada porque eu perdi o ônibus.
Cheguei tarde porque perdi o ônibus.
Eu cheguei tarde porque perdi o ônibus.
exercises.explanation: The reason is an event, so 'porque' is followed by the preterite. 'Atrasado' agrees with the speaker's gender.

exercises.prompt: Which word begins the question '___ você não avisou?' meaning 'Why did you not let me know?'
exercises.explanation: A question begins with 'por que', two words and no accent. 'Porque' is the answer word, and 'por quê' with an accent comes at the end of a question.

answers: Graças a Deus, ninguém se machucou.
Graças a Deus ninguém se machucou.
exercises.explanation: The result of the story is a complete event, so the preterite. 'Ninguém' carries an accent because it is stressed on the last syllable despite ending in 'em'.

exercises.audio_target: Infelizmente, eu não pude ir à festa.
choices: Unfortunately, I could not go to the party.
Luckily, I went to the party.
Unfortunately, I did not like the party.

exercises.prompt_source: I found out the truth yesterday.
exercises.explanation: Finding out is the moment a state of knowing begins, so the preterite: 'descobri' or 'soube'.

exercises.audio_target: Enquanto eu cozinhava, a luz apagou.
exercises.hint_source: While I was cooking, the power went out.
